questions.q: How does this lesson define an integration boundary?
options: A firewall rule that blocks unauthorized network traffic
The explicit line stating which system owns what, and exactly how data crosses between systems
The maximum number of API calls a Salesforce org can make per day
A field-level permission restricting who can edit a record
questions.explain: The lesson defines an integration boundary as a decision about ownership and responsibility -- which system is responsible for what, and exactly how data crosses between them -- that technology then implements.

questions.q: In the Request and Reply pattern, what does the calling org do while waiting for the remote system?
options: It sends the request and immediately moves on without tracking the outcome
It pauses and waits for the remote system to finish before updating its own state based on the response
It reads the remote system's data live at query time without storing a copy
It refreshes its own UI automatically every few seconds regardless of the remote system
questions.explain: Request and Reply is a synchronous pattern -- Salesforce invokes a process on a remote system, waits for completion, and only then updates its own state based on the response, such as waiting to confirm a payment authorization.

questions.q: Which integration pattern does this lesson describe as avoiding reconciliation work by never storing a second copy of external data at all?
options: Batch Data Synchronization
Fire and Forget
Data Virtualization
Remote Call-In
questions.explain: Data Virtualization reads external data live at query time rather than storing a local copy, which is exactly what lets it skip the reconciliation work that a replicated copy would otherwise require.

questions.q: In the Remote Call-In pattern, which side initiates the interaction?
options: Salesforce always initiates, and the external system only ever responds
An external system initiates the call and reads or writes Salesforce records through the platform's own APIs
Neither side initiates -- data moves automatically without any API call
A human user must manually trigger every Remote Call-In interaction
questions.explain: Remote Call-In is specifically the pattern where an external system is the initiator, reaching into Salesforce through its APIs to create, read, update, or delete records -- for example, an ERP pushing a new order into Salesforce.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what mistake does picking an integration technology before understanding the business requirement tend to produce?
options: It always produces the cheapest possible integration, regardless of correctness
Integrations that are technically impressive but operationally wrong, such as real-time infrastructure built for a need that was actually a nightly batch
It has no real downside as long as the technology chosen is modern
It guarantees the integration will exceed Salesforce's API limits
questions.explain: The lesson's explicit warning is that choosing a pattern backward from a favorite tool tends to produce integrations that look impressive but are operationally mismatched to the actual need -- such as real-time infrastructure for what was really a batch requirement.
